strengths: Clear problem motivation with intuitive 'think first, finish strong' solution that addresses practical fixed-budget inference scenarios
Consistent empirical improvements across 12 settings (2 models × 2 benchmarks × 3 budgets), winning in 11/12 cases

Comprehensive analysis beyond accuracy: answer-reach rate analysis reveals delayed commitment behavior, depth-width tradeoff validation, and node-level precision showing 'fewer instances, better answers' regime
Thorough ablation study (Table 2) demonstrates all three components contribute, with ablating any single component typically degrading performance
Strong qualitative analysis with search tree visualizations (Figures 5, 12-13) providing clear insight into algorithmic differences from baselines
Excellent reproducibility support: clear Algorithm 1, detailed hyperparameter specifications, public datasets, open-weight models, and comprehensive implementation details in appendices
Honest discussion of limitations including reward model quality issues (near-binary scores), budget counting methodology, narrow scope, and identified failure cases
weaknesses: Narrow evaluation scope significantly limits generalizability: only mathematical reasoning tasks with no evaluation on other domains (QA, NLI, code, summarization); only small models (≤8B), unclear if benefits translate to larger models or if proposed mechanisms are generally applicable

Modest absolute accuracy improvements: gains typically 0.01-0.07 across settings, with some minimal improvements (e.g., Qwen AIME at 20K: 0.189 vs 0.183); incremental nature raises questions about practical significance

Ad-hoc design choices lack principled justification: (1) functional form for ρ-annealing not motivated (why ρ vs ρ² or other schedules?), (2) depth-bias scaling by (1-ρ) unexplained, (3) κ=λ=1 set uniformly without sensitivity analysis, (4) dˆans estimation heuristic somewhat arbitrary

Heavy dependence on reward model quality with insufficient analysis: GenPRM-7B acknowledged to produce near-binary scores with sparse reward landscape, limiting its discriminative power; method's effectiveness likely highly dependent on reward quality but this sensitivity unexplored, hurting generalizability

Incomplete and potentially unfair baseline comparisons: AB-MCTS-M significantly underperforms (attributed to different evaluation setting), weakening comparison; LiteSearch uses different evaluation methodology (Appendix C's per-instance vs dynamic aggregation) potentially favoring BG-MCTS

Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests despite only 3 runs; unclear which differences are statistically meaningful vs noise; small variations (e.g., 0.465 vs 0.443) lack significance indicators
Limited hyperparameter analysis: κ and λ both fixed to 1 without sensitivity study; exploration constant c only briefly tuned; robustness to these choices unexplored

Lack of theoretical justification: no formal analysis for why this particular budget annealing schedule is optimal or why MCTS conditioning is superior to alternatives (adaptive branching, dynamic depth limits)

Reproducibility gaps: no code release mentioned despite paper's focus on practical deployment; virtual generative child mechanism could be more algorithmically precise; exact backpropagation details sparse
Design novelty limited: while the combination is novel, individual components (PUCT annealing, depth biasing, variance-based widening) are relatively straightforward extensions of standard MCTS

Consistent empirical results across 12 settings (2 models × 2 benchmarks × 3 budgets), achieving best accuracy in 11 and second-best in 1, with strong peaks at budget exhaustion

Insightful analysis revealing the 'fewer-instances-but-better-answers' regime with clear depth-width trade-offs and qualitative tree structure visualizations that effectively illustrate behavior shifts

Well-articulated presentation with clear motivation, effective visualizations (Figures 1, 5, 12-13), and comprehensive appendices including prompts and methodology details

Modest improvements in several cases (Llama MATH500 10K: 0.393 vs 0.333 for MCTS) and low absolute performance (Qwen AIME 30K: 0.189) suggest limited practical impact despite consistency

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: identifies and addresses the mismatch between fixed token budgets and budget-agnostic tree-search policies in real deployments
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MATH500, AIME24/25, UGPhysics), models (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-32B), and budget levels with consistent improvements
Thorough empirical analysis with ablations (Table 2), depth-width tradeoff characterization (Figures 6, 12-13), qualitative visualizations (Figures 7, 15-18), and hyperparameter sensitivity (Table 6)
Clear methodology and presentation with effective communication of the wide-to-deep search pattern through figures and tree visualizations
Practical relevance for token-metered API deployments where per-query budgets are fixed, addressing real deployment scenarios
Solid reproducibility with detailed prompts (Appendix E), hyperparameter search documentation (Appendix B), and multiple experimental runs
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is incremental, essentially adding budget-dependence ρ to standard PUCT; three mechanisms (Eqs. 3-6) are straightforward modifications lacking strong theoretical justification

Incomplete budget accounting: method only tracks output tokens, excluding input tokens and reward model computation which can be substantial in practice; limits practical applicability for true cost-aware deployment

Weak reward signal acknowledged but unaddressed: GenPRM-7B produces highly saturated near-binary scores (Table 10, Appendix K with p50≈0.997), fundamentally limiting fine-grained node discrimination; paper doesn't explore benefits with better-calibrated models

Mixed baseline performance raises fairness concerns: AB-MCTS-M (recent NeurIPS 2025 method) significantly underperforms simple Repeated Sampling; paper attributes to 'regime mismatch' without investigation; LiteSearch also underperforms despite being budget-aware

Moderate absolute improvements: AIME24/25 with Llama-3.1-8B shows ~3% gain (0.067→0.087); highest Qwen3-32B accuracy still only 0.350 at 30K budget; no statistical significance testing

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem: The paper identifies a genuine deployment challenge where fixed token budgets are treated merely as stopping conditions rather than actively shaping search behavior. This is highly relevant for metered API settings.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Evaluation across 3 datasets (MATH500, AIME24/25, UGPhysics), 3 LLMs (Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-32B), and 3 budget levels (10K-30K) with consistent improvements (often substantial, e.g., +0.059 on MATH500 at 20K for Qwen2.5-7B vs MCTS).

Clear and intuitive approach: The core insight (broad early exploration → deep refinement) is well-articulated through conceptual diagrams, equations, and especially tree visualizations that convincingly demonstrate the intended wide-to-deep behavior (Figs. 7, 15-16).

Thorough empirical analysis: Excellent supplementary analysis of depth-width trade-offs (Figs. 6, 12-13), answer-reach rates over budget (Figs. 4, 11), ablation study (Table 2), and qualitative tree comparisons demonstrating the method works as intended.

Strong reproducibility: Detailed algorithm description, extensive appendices with prompts, hyperparameter search procedures, evaluation protocols, and implementation details sufficient for reproduction.
Good presentation and writing: Generally clear and well-organized with effective visualizations. The paper is accessible and logical in progression from motivation to implementation.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Technical contributions are incremental—combining standard MCTS ideas (exploration annealing by ρ, depth-biased value correction, virtual generative nodes) without significant algorithmic innovation. The ad-hoc nature of Eq. 5 (why linear in depth? why κ(1-ρ) scaling?) lacks strong justification.

Weak reward signal undermines evaluation confidence: GenPRM-7B scores are highly saturated and near-binary (p75≈0.999, Table 10), providing weak fine-grained feedback. While this doesn't affect comparison fairness, it raises questions whether improvements would persist with better-calibrated PRMs. This critical limitation is relegated to Section 6/Appendix K rather than emphasized in main results.

Incomplete baseline investigation: (1) AB-MCTS-M dramatically underperforms (0.542 vs 0.699 on Qwen2.5-7B), attributed to 'regime mismatch' without deeper investigation or hyperparameter verification. (2) LiteSearch handicapping—disabling greedy pre-generation to align token counting may disadvantage LiteSearch. (3) Missing simple budget-aware baselines (fixed depth/width limits, naive annealing).

Narrow evaluation scope: (1) Limited to reasoning tasks—generalization to other domains (summarization, QA, code) unclear. (2) Only tested on models ≤32B; unclear for frontier models. (3) Budget range limited to 10K-30K tokens; behavior at very different scales unknown. (4) UGPhysics uses different evaluation paradigm (rollout-based), smaller dataset (120 questions), and only 2 models.

Lack of theoretical grounding: No formal analysis of why budget-conditioning helps, convergence properties, or conditions for expected benefits. The exploration-exploitation argument could be formalized. Missing analysis of when the method might fail.

Limited hyperparameter analysis: Sensitivity analysis (Table 6) shown for only one model/dataset at 20K budget. No analysis across different budgets or task difficulties. Default values (c=√2, κ=1, λ=1) justified for standard MCTS but not why these are optimal for BG-MCTS.
Missing computational cost analysis: No discussion of overhead from maintaining ρ, computing depth-biased values, managing virtual nodes. Query latency matters for deployment but is not analyzed.

Coverage-quality tradeoff not empirically validated: Section L.2 discusses potential benefits for data synthesis but doesn't empirically verify with downstream model training. Lower coverage on single-solution settings could be problematic depending on use case.

Statistical rigor concerns: Results averaged over 'three trials' without confidence intervals or significance tests. Some improvements modest (Llama 10K: 0.393 vs 0.406). No formal statistical testing for claimed improvements.

Incomplete baseline fairness analysis: Budget accounting for LiteSearch (Appendix C) is complex; the 'budget-redistributed aggregation' for plots is creative but whether it's entirely fair to LiteSearch is debatable. AB-MCTS-M's poor performance deserves investigation rather than attribution to regime mismatch.
